mainTopic: Claims after a death (deposits and a gift 'to טוביה'), and forgiving a sold debt
overview: This amud opens with the last words of an earlier discussion: a document that only looks false is not a concern. Then the גמרא tells three matching stories. In each, a man deposited a valuable item with someone who died without saying whose it was. Each judge, רבי אמי, רב נחמן and רבי אבא, gives the item to the claimant, because the dead man was known not to be wealthy and the claimant gave a סימן (identifying sign). Each time the גמרא adds that a סימן helps only if the claimant was not a regular visitor to that house. Next comes a man who left his property 'to טוביה.' The גמרא rules on who counts as that טוביה: a man titled רב, a close friend, and how to rank a תלמיד חכם, a neighbor and a relative. When the two are equal, the judges decide (שודא דדייני). Then רבא quotes רב חייא בר אבין: שמואל lets a seller of a שטר חוב forgive the debt, but agrees that a wife cannot forgive a note she brought into her marriage. The amud ends with a relative of רב נחמן who sold her כתובה, and רב נחמן asks whether anyone will advise her daughter. The advice comes on the next amud.

steps.title: The end of the earlier discussion: something that only looks false is not a concern
steps.stepSummary: The closing line of the previous discussion. Something in a document that merely looks like a falsehood is not a problem.
steps.simpleTranslation: We are not concerned about something that only looks like a falsehood.
steps.whatsHappening: These are the final words of the previous discussion. The גמרא finishes by saying that a document that only appears false is not a concern.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier discussion dealt with a document written before the event it describes. The conclusion is that this only looks like שקר (a falsehood) but is not really a lie, so we do not worry about it. This closes that topic before the new stories begin.

keyTerms.meaning: Like a falsehood, only looking false
We are not concerned, we do not worry about it

phrases.english: About something that looks like a falsehood, we are not concerned.
phrases.notes: This wraps up the earlier discussion about a document written ahead of time. It only looks false, so it's not a real problem.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the discussion from the previous part of the daf.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A document that only appears false, because it was written early, is not treated as a lie.

steps.title: A man deposits seven pearls with רבי מיאשא, who dies without instructions
steps.stepSummary: A man left seven pearls wrapped in a sheet at רבי מיאשא's house. רבי מיאשא died without saying whose they were, and the case came to רבי אמי.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man deposited seven pearls tied up in a sheet in the house of רבי מיאשא, the grandson of רבי יהושע בן לוי. רבי מיאשא died without leaving instructions. They came before רבי אמי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new story and sets up the case. The ruling comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem is that the only person who knew the truth, the one holding the pearls, has died. His family could say the pearls belonged to him, while the man claims they are his. A judge must now decide without testimony from the dead man.

keyTerms.meaning: And he did not give instructions before dying

phrases.english: There was a certain man who deposited
seven pearls that were tied up in a sheet
in the house of Rabbi Meyasha,

phrases.aramaic: בַּר בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי.
phrases.english: the grandson of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.
Rabbi Meyasha died and did not leave instructions.
They came before Rabbi Ami.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: claims to a deposit after the holder's death.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The case is set up: the claimant says the pearls are his, and the holder died without explaining.

steps.title: רבי אמי rules for the claimant: the dead man was not wealthy, and the claimant gave a sign
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי gives the pearls to the claimant for two reasons. רבי מיאשא was known not to be wealthy, and the claimant gave a סימן.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: First, I know about רבי מיאשא, the grandson of רבי יהושע בן לוי, that he was not wealthy. And furthermore, this man is giving an identifying sign.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אמי decides the case. He gives the pearls to the man who claims them and offers two reasons.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Reason one: a man who was not wealthy would not likely own seven pearls, so they probably are not his. Reason two: the claimant can describe identifying details, which shows he knows the item. The two reasons together make the claim believable.

phrases.english: He said to them: First,
I know about Rabbi Meyasha,

phrases.aramaic: בַּר בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי
phrases.english: the grandson of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi,
that he was not wealthy.
And furthermore, this man is giving an identifying sign.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the ruling for the case set up in step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The item goes to the claimant when the dead holder was known not to be wealthy and the claimant gives a סימן.

steps.title: Limit: the sign only works if the claimant did not regularly visit that house
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא limits רבי אמי's ruling. If the claimant often went in and out of that house, his סימן proves nothing, because he may have just seen someone else's deposit.
steps.simpleTranslation: We only said this when he is not used to going in and out of there. But if he is used to going in and out of there, say that someone else deposited it, and he just saw it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a limit to the ruling it just gave. A סימן is only trusted when the claimant was not a frequent visitor in that house.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A סימן is meant to show that you are the owner. A frequent visitor could know what the item looks like just from seeing it there, even if a different person deposited it. In that case the סימן no longer proves ownership.

keyTerms.meaning: We only said this when, introduces a limit

steps.whatToRemember: A סימן proves ownership only if the claimant had no other way of knowing what the item looks like. A regular visitor to the house could have learned the signs just by seeing it.
steps.confusionAlert: This limit does not mean the claimant is lying. It only means his סימן is not proof, because a frequent visitor could know the signs without being the owner.

phrases.english: And we only said this
when he is not used to going in and out of there.
phrases.notes: "There" means the house of the man who died.

phrases.english: But if he is used to going in and out of there,
say that a different person deposited it,
and he just saw it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the ruling of step 3 by limiting when a סימן is effective.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A סימן does not help a claimant who regularly entered the house, since he may have just seen another person's deposit.

steps.title: A second case: a silver cup deposited with חסא, who dies without instructions
steps.stepSummary: A man left a silver cup at חסא's house. חסא died without saying whose it was, and the case came to רב נחמן.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man deposited a silver cup in the house of חסא. חסא died without leaving instructions. They came before רב נחמן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second story that matches the first one. It sets up the case, and the ruling comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The situation is the same as before: a valuable item, a holder who died, and no instructions. Bringing a second judge's ruling on the same kind of case shows that this approach was accepted by more than one authority.

keyTerms.meaning: חסא, the name of the man who held the cup

phrases.english: There was a certain man who deposited
a silver cup in the house of Chasa.
Chasa died and did not leave instructions.
They came before Rav Nachman.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel story to the case in step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The case is set up: the claimant says the cup is his, and the holder died without explaining.

steps.title: רב נחמן rules the same way: חסא was not wealthy, and the claimant gave a sign
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן gives the cup to the claimant for the same two reasons רבי אמי used.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: I know about חסא that he was not wealthy. And furthermore, this man is giving an identifying sign.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן decides the second case. He gives the same two reasons that רבי אמי gave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Again, a man without wealth would not likely own a silver cup, and the claimant's סימן supports his claim. The matching reasons show that both judges followed the same method.

phrases.english: He said to them: I know about Chasa
that he was not wealthy.
And furthermore, this man is giving an identifying sign.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the ruling for step 5, matching the ruling in step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The cup goes to the claimant because חסא was not wealthy and the claimant gave a סימן.

steps.title: The same limit applies: a regular visitor's sign proves nothing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא repeats the limit. If the claimant often visited חסא's house, his סימן does not help, since he may have just seen someone else's deposit.
steps.simpleTranslation: We only said this when he is not used to going in and out of there. But if he is used to going in and out of there, say that someone else deposited it, and he just saw it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats the same limit for רב נחמן's case. It again explains that a frequent visitor's סימן is not proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The limit is attached to each story separately, so it is clear that both rulings depend on it. The rule is the same in both cases: a סימן counts only when the claimant could not have learned it just by seeing the item.

keyTerms.meaning: To there, meaning the dead man's house

steps.whatToRemember: In both stories, the claimant wins when the holder was not wealthy and the claimant gives a סימן. In both, a סימן does not help if the claimant regularly visited that house.

phrases.english: And we only said this
when he is not used to going in and out of there.
But if he is used to going in and out of there,
say that a different person deposited it,
and he just saw it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies to רב נחמן's ruling the same limit that step 4 applied to רבי אמי's ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A claimant who regularly entered the house cannot rely on a סימן, since he may have just seen another person's deposit.

steps.title: Silk left at רב דימי's house
steps.stepSummary: A man deposited silk with רב דימי, brother of רב ספרא. רב דימי died without saying whose silk it was.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man deposited silk at the house of רב דימי, the brother of רב ספרא. רב דימי died and gave no instructions about it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a third story just like the pearls and the silver cup. This line sets up the case; the ruling comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The details match the earlier stories: a deposit, a keeper who died, and no instructions. That is why we expect the same two-reason ruling to follow.

keyTerms.meaning: And he did not give instructions

phrases.english: A certain man who deposited silk

phrases.aramaic: בֵּי רַב דִּימִי אֲחוּהּ דְּרַב סָפְרָא,
phrases.english: at the house of Rav Dimi, brother of Rav Safra.
Rav Dimi died and did not give instructions.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא דְּאַפְקֵיד מְטַכְסָא בֵּי רַב דִּימִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third parallel case after רבי אמי's pearls and רב נחמן's cup.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the case: silk deposited with רב דימי, who died without instructions.

steps.title: רבי אבא gives the silk to the claimant
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא rules for the claimant. רב דימי was known not to be wealthy, and the claimant gave a סימן.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case came before רבי אבא. He said: First, I know that רב דימי was not wealthy. Also, the claimant is giving a סימן.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא gives the silk to the claimant. He uses the same two reasons as רבי אמי and רב נחמן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since רב דימי was not wealthy, the silk is unlikely to be his own, so his heirs have a weak claim. The סימן then shows that this claimant really is the owner. A third case with the same reasoning shows this is a fixed approach.

phrases.english: He came before Rabbi Abba.
He said to them: First,

phrases.aramaic: דְּיָדַעְנָא בֵּיהּ בְּרַב דִּימִי דְּלָא אֲמִיד.
phrases.english: I know about Rav Dimi that he was not wealthy.
And furthermore, he is giving an identifying sign.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the ruling for the case set up in step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The silk goes to the claimant: the keeper was not wealthy, and the claimant gave a סימן.

steps.title: The same limit applies to the silk case
steps.stepSummary: The ruling holds only if the claimant did not often visit the house. If he did, his סימן proves nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: We only said this when he did not usually go in and out of that house. But if he did, we can say someone else deposited it and he just saw it.
steps.whatsHappening: For the third time, the גמרא adds the same limit to the ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A סימן only proves ownership if the claimant had no other way to know the details. A frequent visitor could have learned what the item looked like by seeing someone else's deposit.

keyTerms.meaning: We only said this when... (a limit on a ruling)
Used to going in and out (a frequent visitor)

steps.whatToRemember: In all three stories, the claimant wins when two things are true: the keeper was known not to be wealthy, and the claimant gives a סימן. The סימן only counts if he was not a regular visitor at the keeper's house.

phrases.english: And we said this only
when he does not usually go in and out there.
But if he usually goes in and out there,
say that another person deposited it,
and he merely saw it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא דְּלָא רְגִיל דְּעָיֵיל וְנָפֵיק לְהָתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits רבי אבא's ruling, the same way steps 4 and 7 limited the earlier rulings.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A frequent visitor's סימן does not prove ownership.

steps.title: 'My property to טוביה' and טוביה shows up
steps.stepSummary: A dying man left his property to טוביה. A man named טוביה came, and רבי יוחנן said, 'Here, טוביה has come.'
steps.simpleTranslation: A man said, 'My property goes to טוביה,' and then died. A טוביה came. רבי יוחנן said: Here, טוביה has come.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic: a gift that names a person only by first name. רבי יוחנן rules that the טוביה who shows up gets the property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We do not worry that the dying man meant some other טוביה. A person with that name came forward, so he gets the property.

keyTerms.meaning: Here, טוביה has come (he is the one meant)

phrases.english: A certain man who said to them:
My property should go to Toviya.
He died, and Toviya came.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: הֲרֵי בָּא טוֹבִיָּה.
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said: Here, Toviya has come.
phrases.notes: He means we accept this טוביה and don't worry about some other person with the same name.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story about identifying the person a dying man named.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person named טוביה who comes forward receives the property.

steps.title: רב טוביה is not plain 'טוביה'
steps.stepSummary: If a man called רב טוביה comes forward, he does not get the property. The dying man said 'טוביה,' not 'רב טוביה.'
steps.simpleTranslation: If he said 'טוביה' and רב טוביה came, he does not get it. He said 'to טוביה'; he did not say 'to רב טוביה.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a limit to רבי יוחנן's ruling. A man known by the title 'רב' is not the plain 'טוביה' who was named.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person known as רב טוביה would normally be called by his title. Since the dying man left the title out, we assume he meant a different person.

phrases.english: If he said 'Toviya' and Rav Toviya came,
he said 'to Toviya,'
he did not say 'to Rav Toviya.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits רבי יוחנן's ruling: the title 'רב' makes it a different name.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב טוביה does not receive a gift left to plain 'טוביה'.

steps.title: A close friend may be called without his title
steps.stepSummary: If רב טוביה was close with the dying man, he does get the property, because a friend uses a plain name.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he was a person who was close with him, then he was close with him, and he would have called him just 'טוביה.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא makes an exception to the previous step. A close friend gets the property even though he has a title.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Leaving out the title only matters if the dying man would normally have used it. Close friends call each other by first name, so in that case 'טוביה' can mean רב טוביה.

keyTerms.meaning: Who is close and familiar with him

phrases.english: But if he is a person who is close with him,
then he was close with him.
phrases.notes: He means that close friends skip titles, so plain 'טוביה' fits רב טוביה here.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: An exception to step 12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A close friend named רב טוביה can receive a gift left to 'טוביה'.

steps.title: Two people named טוביה: the תלמיד חכם comes first
steps.stepSummary: If two men named טוביה come, the תלמיד חכם wins over a neighbor. He also wins over a relative.
steps.simpleTranslation: If two men named טוביה came, one a neighbor and one a תלמיד חכם, the תלמיד חכם comes first. If one is a relative and one is a תלמיד חכם, the תלמיד חכם comes first.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now handles two people with the same name. It ranks a תלמיד חכם above both a neighbor and a relative.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The goal is to figure out which טוביה the dying man most likely meant. The גמרא assumes he would most likely want his property to go to a תלמיד חכם, ahead of a neighbor or relative.

phrases.english: If two men named Toviya came,
a neighbor and a Torah scholar,
the Torah scholar comes first.
A relative and a Torah scholar,
the Torah scholar comes first.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new situation in the טוביה case: two people with the same name.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A תלמיד חכם has priority over a neighbor and over a relative.

steps.title: Neighbor or relative: who comes first?
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים ask what the rule is when one טוביה is a neighbor and the other is a relative.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: a neighbor and a relative, what is the rule?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a real question that the previous rules did not answer. The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 14 only compared each of them to a תלמיד חכם. It never compared the neighbor and the relative to each other.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was raised before them

phrases.english: It was asked of them:
A neighbor and a relative, what is the rule?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about a pairing step 14 did not cover; step 16 answers it.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a neighbor or a relative has priority when both are named טוביה.

steps.title: A פסוק: a close neighbor is better
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers from משלי: 'Better a close neighbor than a distant brother.' The neighbor comes first.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: 'Better is a close neighbor than a distant brother.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with a פסוק. It shows that a neighbor comes before a relative.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק shows that a neighbor who is close by matters more than a relative who is far away. So the neighbor gets the property.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
'Better is a close neighbor than a distant brother.'

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע טוֹב שָׁכֵן קָרוֹב מֵאָח רָחוֹק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The neighbor has priority over the relative, based on משלי 27:10.

steps.title: When both are equal, the judges decide
steps.stepSummary: If both men are relatives, both are neighbors, or both are חכמים, there is no rule. The judges decide.
steps.simpleTranslation: If both are relatives, both are neighbors, or both are scholars? It is left to the judges' discretion.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends the topic. When nothing makes one טוביה stand out, the decision is left to the judges.
steps.deeperAnalysis: All the earlier rules work by finding one thing that makes one person a better fit. When both men are the same in every way that counts, there is no fixed rule. The judges simply decide.

keyTerms.meaning: The judges' discretion: they decide as they see fit

steps.whatToRemember: How to rank two people named טוביה: a תלמיד חכם comes before a neighbor or a relative, and a neighbor comes before a relative. If the two are equal, the judges decide.

phrases.english: If both are relatives,
or both are neighbors,
or both are scholars?
It is the judges' discretion.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁנֵיהֶם קְרוֹבִים וּשְׁנֵיהֶם שְׁכֵנִים וּשְׁנֵיהֶם חֲכָמִים שׁוּדָא דְּדַיָּינֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the ranking rules by covering the case where the two are equal.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: When both claimants are equal, the decision is left to the judges' discretion (שודא דדייני).

steps.title: רבא quotes שמואל's rule about forgiving a sold loan document
steps.stepSummary: רבא tells the son of רב חייא בר אבין that he will share his father's excellent teaching. The teaching builds on שמואל's rule: a lender who sold a שטר חוב can still forgive the debt, and so can his heir.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to the son of רב חייא בר אבין: Come, I will tell you an excellent thing your father used to say. It is about what שמואל said: If someone sells a loan document to another person and then forgives the debt, it is forgiven. Even the seller's heir can forgive it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. רבא quotes שמואל's rule as background, and this sets up the new teaching that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל holds that selling a loan document does not stop the original lender from forgiving the debt. The forgiveness still works, so the buyer is left with nothing to collect. Even the lender's heir has this power.

keyTerms.meaning: A loan document, the written proof of a debt
It is forgiven, and the debt is gone

steps.confusionAlert: Even though the lender sold the document, his forgiveness still cancels the debt. The buyer, not the debtor, is the one who loses.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא לִבְרֵיהּ דְּרַב חִיָּיא בַּר אָבִין:
phrases.english: Rava said to the son of Rav Chiyya bar Avin:
Come, I will tell you an excellent thing
that your father used to say.
About that which Shmuel said:
One who sells a loan document to another person
and then went back and forgave it, it is forgiven,
and even an heir can forgive it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: New topic. The case of the two people named טוביה has ended.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A lender who sold a שטר חוב can still forgive the debt, and so can his heir.

steps.title: שמואל agrees a wife cannot forgive a note she brought into the marriage
steps.stepSummary: רב חייא בר אבין's teaching: שמואל agrees that if a woman brought a loan document into her marriage and later forgave the debt, the forgiveness does not work. Her husband has equal rights in it.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל agrees about a woman who brings a loan document into the marriage for her husband and then forgives the debt: it is not forgiven, because his hand is like her hand.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the excellent teaching רבא promised. It gives a case where שמואל's rule from Step 18 does not apply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 18, the seller has no partner, so he can cancel the debt by himself. Here the husband shares her rights in the document, so she cannot cancel it alone. This is an exception to the rule, not a disagreement with it.

keyTerms.meaning: Agrees (that his rule has an exception)
A woman who brings property into her marriage
His hand is like her hand, so he has equal rights

steps.whatToRemember: A seller can forgive a debt he sold (Step 18). A wife cannot forgive a note she brought into the marriage, because her husband shares the rights to it.

phrases.aramaic: מוֹדֶה שְׁמוּאֵל בְּמַכְנֶסֶת שְׁטַר חוֹב לְבַעְלָהּ,
phrases.english: Shmuel agrees about a woman who brings a loan document into the marriage for her husband,
and then she went back and forgave it,
that it is not forgiven,
because his hand is like her hand.
phrases.notes: He means the husband has the same rights in the document as she does, so she can't cancel it alone.

steps.triggerLanguage: מוֹדֶה שְׁמוּאֵל בְּמַכְנֶסֶת שְׁטַר חוֹב לְבַעְלָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits שמואל's rule from Step 18 with an exception.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A wife's forgiveness of a note she brought into the marriage does not work, because her husband shares the rights to it.

steps.title: רב נחמן's relative sold her כתובה, then was divorced and died
steps.stepSummary: A relative of רב נחמן sold the rights to her כתובה for a small payment. Later she was divorced and died, and the buyers demanded the money from her daughter.
steps.simpleTranslation: A relative of רב נחמן sold her כתובה for a small payment. She was divorced and then died. The buyers came and claimed the money from her daughter.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story that tests the rule about forgiving a sold debt. Here it lays out the facts of the case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The buyers had paid for the chance to collect the כתובה if she were divorced. She was divorced, so the כתובה could now be collected. After she died, her rights passed to her daughter, so the buyers went to the daughter.

keyTerms.meaning: The marriage contract that promises the wife money if she is divorced or widowed
A small payment for a possible future benefit

phrases.english: A relative of Rav Nachman
sold her ketubah for a small payment.
phrases.notes: She got a little money now for the chance that the buyer would collect the כתובה later, if she was ever divorced.

phrases.english: She was divorced and died.
They came and claimed it from her daughter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A real story that relates to the rule about forgiving a sold debt.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Facts of the case: a sold כתובה, then divorce and death, and the buyers claim from the daughter.

steps.title: רב נחמן asks if anyone will advise the daughter
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן calls out to the people around him: is there no one who will give the daughter advice? The advice itself comes on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said to them: Is there no one who can give her advice?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן hints that the daughter has a way to protect herself. This line sets up the advice that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Based on שמואל's rule in Step 18, the daughter, as heir, has a way out of paying the buyers. רב נחמן's question points toward that solution without saying it yet.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said to them:
Is there no one who can give her advice?!
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets, לָהּ, and some leave it out. The meaning is the same either way.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story by setting up רב נחמן's advice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב נחמן hints that the daughter has a way to avoid paying the buyers.
